Levy
LEV-ee
noun
From the French lever, to raise, through the Latin levare, to lift; hence a raising — of men for labour or war, or of money or goods as a tribute. The Authorized Version uses it chiefly of Solomon’s conscripted labour and of the tribute raised unto the LORD from the spoil.

Biblical Definition

A levy is a raising — of men, of goods, or of money — exacted by authority. Scripture uses the word in two very different keys. The first is holy: after the war with Midian the LORD commands, “levy a tribute unto the LORD of the men of war which went out to battle: one soul of five hundred” (Num 31:28), with a heavier portion of fifty from the congregation’s half given to the Levites (Num 31:30). Here the levy confesses that the victory and the spoil were God’s before they were Israel’s, and that the first fruit of every increase belongs to Him. The second key is grave. “King Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men” (1Ki 5:13), sent by courses to Lebanon under Adoniram, and the chronicler explains its purpose: to build the house of the LORD, and Solomon’s own house, and Millo, and the walls of Jerusalem and the fortified cities (1Ki 9:15). The temple was built by it; so was the king’s magnificence. Samuel had warned exactly this when Israel demanded a king like the nations: he will take your sons, and your fields, and your vineyards, and ye shall cry out in that day (1Sa 8:11–18). The reckoning came at Shechem, when Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute, and all Israel stoned him (1Ki 12:18), and the kingdom tore in two. A levy for God is worship; a levy that consumes the people for a king’s glory ends in stones.

Webster 1828 Definition

A raising or collecting — of troops, forced labourers, or tribute; in Scripture both the holy portion levied unto the LORD and Solomon’s conscription that broke the kingdom.

expand to see more

LEVY, n. [French lever, to raise; L. levare.] The act of raising men for military service; troops so raised.

The act of collecting money by authority; a tax, tribute, or exaction so raised.

In the Scriptures, the body of men raised by Solomon for forced labour (1Ki 5:13; 9:15).

To levy war, to raise or begin war; to take arms for attack.

To levy a tribute unto the LORD, to set apart His portion out of the spoil (Num 31:28).

Key Scripture

1Ki 5:13 — "And king Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men."

1Ki 9:15 — "And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer."

Num 31:28 — "And levy a tribute unto the LORD of the men of war which went out to battle: one soul of five hundred, both of the persons, and of the beeves, and of the asses, and of the sheep:"

1Sa 8:14 — "And he will take your fields, and your vineyards, and your oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants."

Modern Corruption

Solomon’s levy is read as mere administrative history, and Samuel’s warning about what kings take is quietly detached from the state that takes far more today.

expand to see more

The corruption here is not a modern redefinition of the word but a modern deafness to the text. Samuel’s speech in 1Sa 8 is a plain prophecy of what centralised power does: it takes sons, daughters, fields, vineyards, oliveyards, servants and a tenth of the increase, and the people who asked for it will cry out and not be heard. The chronicler shows the prophecy fulfilled in Israel’s wisest king, whose levy of thirty thousand built both the temple and Millo, and in his son, whose promise to add to the yoke cost him ten tribes. Scripture treats the family, the church, and the civil magistrate as three distinct authorities under God, each bounded; a levy is lawful within the magistrate’s sphere — render tribute to whom tribute is due (Rom 13:7) — and unlawful when it swallows the other spheres and the man’s inheritance with them. Reading Solomon’s levy as neutral bureaucracy loses the warning God troubled to record twice.

Recover the levy unto the LORD as the pattern of every rightful claim upon a man’s substance. God’s portion out of the Midianite spoil was small — one of five hundred from the soldiers, one of fifty from the congregation — and it was rendered gladly because the whole was His gift. Where a claim is God’s, it is worship; where it is Caesar’s and lawful, it is duty; where it is a king’s appetite dressed as necessity, it is the thing Samuel warned of and Rehoboam learned too late. Give God His portion first, pay the magistrate what is honestly due, and do not confuse the two.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A raising of men or goods by authority; holy when levied unto the LORD, ruinous when a king consumes his people to build his own house.

expand to see more

Levy — French lever, Latin levare, to raise or lift up.

Hebrew mas, a burden or forced-labour gang (1Ki 5:13; 9:15; 12:18).

Adoniram, and after him Adoram, was over the levy — and was stoned for it (1Ki 12:18).

Num 31:28 uses the verb of God’s own portion out of the spoil of Midian.

Samuel’s warning (1Sa 8:11–18) is the interpretive key to Solomon’s levy.

Usage

"Distinguish the levy unto the LORD from the levy out of Israel — one is worship, the other burden."

"The temple and Millo were built by the same gangs; note that Scripture records both purposes together."

"Rehoboam’s tribute-officer stoned at Shechem is the historical verdict on an unrelieved yoke."
